messages.subject: Problem:  All samples are the exact same value !?!?
parts:
Hi,

Thanks to some good advice from Andrew and Ben, I was able to get my model compiled and running in stan (From the command line.)

The code is running painfully slow, on a fairly robust machine (Core i7, 32GB RAM, Linux, etc.) 

However, after 43 hours, it is about 50% complete.  Curious to see what some of the samples looked like, I had a look at the samples.csv output file.  Much to my surprise, all of the samples appear to have the exact same values.  All of them - the same. 

Clearly, I've made a mistake in my model design somewhere.  My intent is to have a hierarchical model looking student enrollment, which effects for the student's "group" and the "program".  (10 groups, 27 programs) 

I've pasted the model below and would really appreciate any suggestions. 

Thank You

======================================================================
data {
    int<lower=1> N; // number of tracts
    int<lower=1> n_group; // number of groups
    int n_prog; // number of programs

    int<lower=0> count[N];
    int<lower=1> group[N]; 
    int<lower=1> program[N];

    real var_1[N];
    real var_2[N];
    real var_3[N];
   

}
parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_group;
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_program;

    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_var_1;
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_var_2;
    real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_var_3;
   
    real<lower=0>  group_effect[n_group];
    real<lower=0>  prog_effect[n_prog];

    real b_var_1;
    real b_var_2;
    real b_var_3;
   
}

model {

    b_var_1 ~ normal(0, sigma_var_1);
    b_var_2 ~ normal(0, sigma_var_2);
    b_var_3 ~ normal(0, sigma_var_3);
   

    for(j in 1:n_group){
        group_effect[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_group);
    }

    for(j in 1:n_prog){
        prog_effect[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_program);
    }

    for(n in 1:N){
        real eta[N];

        eta[n] <- group_effect[group[n]]
            + prog_effect[program[n]]
            + b_var_1 * var_1[n]
            + b_var_2 * var_2[n]
            + b_var_3 * var_3[n];

        count[n] ~ poisson(exp( eta[n] ));
    }
}

Thanks to some good advice from Andrew and Ben, I was able to get my model compiled and running in stan (From the command line.)

The code is running painfully slow, on a fairly robust machine (Core i7, 32GB RAM, Linux, etc.)

The hardware has less to do with the wall time than the software, and you've coded it in the slowest possible way for a model like this. The only real benefit for a CPU like that is that you can do 8 chains at once.

However, after 43 hours, it is about 50% complete.  Curious to see what some of the samples looked like, I had a look at the samples.csv output file.  Much to my surprise, all of the samples appear to have the exact same values.  All of them - the same.

The only thing that I can see that is really wrong with your code is that real eta[N] should be declared at the start of the model {} block, rather than inside that loop, i.e.

model {
  real eta[N];
  ...

but I don't think that would cause all the proposals to get rejected. I suspect that the default starting values are inappropriate for your data, but even then I wouldn't expect every proposal to be rejected.

So, I would try taking out the group and program effects. If that model runs, add the group effects back. If that model runs, add the program effects back. Etc. That will help you narrow down the problem.

Ben

On Sunday, December 2, 2012 2:35:41 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
I still have  a lot to learn about hierarchical models.

Will try your suggestions and report back to the group what I find.

It's not so much about hierarchical models in the statistical sense; it is more about understanding the differences between a Gibbs sampler like BUGS and a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler, particularly one like Stan that utilizes auto-differentiation. There's not a whole lot that can be done to accelerate a BUGS model because it just figures out the corresponding DAG and sequentially samples from each conditional distribution. With Stan, various parameterizations that are statistically equivalent can perform very differently in practice and can take different amounts of time to do so, largely depending on how much burden they put on the auto-differentiation mechanism.

Ben

> so, largely depending on how much burden they put on the auto-differentiation mechanism.

This is all given a particular distribution over parameters
that is being modeled.

The one thing that we can do in Stan that is like what you
can do in BUGS/JAGS is reparameterize. It has a slightly
different effect and motivation for HMC, where
it's largely about making the posterior geometry more friendly,
which is usually an issue of making it more homogeneous in
curvature throughout the posterior probability mass that should
be sampled.

- Bob

parts:
You should also try running with the test_grad option (available
in R and command line versions), which will at least show you
what the initial parameters and gradients look like. If any of
those are NaN or infinite (or close to infinite), it will highlight
where the problem in the model specification is. This should run
quickly unless there are a whole lot of parameters. (The next
version of Stan we release will run the finite differences involved
in test_grad much faster; we should probably also have an option
to turn finite diffs off, which will still allow users to debug
with the analytic auto-diff results from Stan without the time
consumption of finite diffs.)

- Bob

On Sunday, December 2, 2012 4:40:51 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
Ben,

1) I'll try an intercept now and report back.
In addition, it would be good to start the chain with an intercept equal to the log of the mean value of count. Everything else can start at zero or zero on average.
2) What values am i looking for and where in the gradient output?    (I need to learn how to interpret this properly to diagnose things myself.)

What you want to see is a log-posterior value that is something sane (not on the order of -1e70) and that the auto-differentiated gradient is equal to the numerically-differentiated gradient. But numeric derivatives are not going to be accurate when the starting values put you at a virtually flat spot in the log-posterior.

Ben

parts:
On Sunday, December 2, 2012 4:45:08 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
On Sunday, December 2, 2012 4:40:51 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
Ben,

1) I'll try an intercept now and report back.

In addition, it would be good to start the chain with an intercept equal to the log of the mean value of count. Everything else can start at zero or zero on average.

Another thing that could be done is to use a construction like this

transformed data {
  real log_mean_count;
  log_mean_count <- log(mean(count));
}
parameters {
  real intercept_shift;
  ...
}
transformed parameters {
  real intercept;
  intercept <- log_mean_count + intercept_shift;
}
model {
  ...
  for (n in 1:N) {
    eta[n] <- intercept + ...;
    count[n] ~ poisson(exp(eta[n]));
  }
  ...
}

If you do it that way, then the default starting values for Stan should be okay.

Ben
